name: Search, Feed, and Ranking Interview Prep
description: 20 advanced questions on search systems, feeds, ranking, freshness, fanout, recommendation trade-offs, and large-scale retrieval.

cards.front: 1. What is the difference between search and feed systems?
cards.back: Search is usually user-initiated and query-driven, while feeds are proactive and continuously assembled. That difference changes indexing, freshness, and ranking strategy.

cards.front: 2. Why is ranking hard at scale?
cards.back: Because ranking is not just sorting; it mixes relevance, freshness, personalization, safety, and business goals under tight latency budgets. The challenge is choosing the signals that matter most.

cards.front: 3. How do inverted indexes work?
cards.back: They map terms to the documents that contain them, which makes retrieval efficient for text search. The index structure is what turns search from a scan into a lookup problem.

cards.front: 4. What is fanout in feed generation?
cards.back: Fanout pushes new content to many recipients eagerly, while fanout-on-read reconstructs it when the user opens the feed. Each approach trades write cost for read cost differently.

cards.front: 5. When is fanout-on-write better than fanout-on-read?
cards.back: It is better when reads must be very fast and the audience size is manageable. It shifts work to write time, which is often worth it for high-read products.

cards.front: 6. What makes freshness difficult?
cards.back: Freshness competes with cache efficiency, ranking stability, and ingestion cost. In many products, users want both fast updates and stable ranking, which are in tension.

cards.front: 7. Why do feeds often need multiple stages?
cards.back: A candidate generation stage narrows the corpus, then a ranking stage applies richer models to a smaller set. This keeps latency manageable while still supporting sophisticated relevance logic.

cards.front: 8. How do you balance personalization with relevance?
cards.back: Personalization improves engagement but can overfit the user into a narrow bubble or hurt system explainability. Staff-level designs choose a measured blend instead of maximizing one signal blindly.

cards.front: 9. What is the role of deduplication in feeds?
cards.back: Deduping avoids repeated content, redundant notifications, or repeated search results that look broken to users. It is a practical quality filter, not just a nice-to-have.

cards.front: 10. How do you handle ranking latency budgets?
cards.back: Use cheap features first, precompute what you can, and reserve expensive scoring for a small candidate set. Latency budgets force explicit trade-offs between model quality and user experience.

cards.front: 11. Why is relevance evaluation difficult?
cards.back: Because offline metrics do not always match what users actually do in production. A ranking system needs both offline judgment and online experimentation.

cards.front: 12. What is the importance of query understanding?
cards.back: Query understanding improves recall and precision by normalizing intent, synonyms, spelling, and ambiguity. Without it, even a strong index can return the wrong result set.

cards.front: 13. How do you think about abuse in search and feed products?
cards.back: Abuse can manipulate ranking, spam results, or exploit recommendation loops, so safety signals need to be part of the design. Search quality and abuse prevention are tightly linked.

cards.front: 14. What is the cost of stale indexing?
cards.back: Stale indexes produce missing, duplicated, or outdated results that users notice quickly. The system needs a freshness model and a clear ingestion SLA.

cards.front: 15. How do you scale a large feed store?
cards.back: Partition by user or audience, precompute common slices, and keep the hot read path small. The goal is to avoid rebuilding large timelines on demand.

cards.front: 16. What is the trade-off between global and localized ranking?
cards.back: Global ranking can give consistent quality, while localized ranking can account for user or region context better. The best system usually combines shared and context-specific signals.

cards.front: 17. Why are offline precomputations useful?
cards.back: They move expensive work out of the request path and make latency predictable. Precomputation is especially valuable when many users share similar candidate sets or features.

cards.front: 18. How do you decide what to cache in a feed system?
cards.back: Cache the expensive, frequently reused derivations that materially reduce read latency. Caching everything usually just adds staleness and invalidation work.

cards.front: 19. What is the role of experimentation in ranking systems?
cards.back: A ranking change should be validated with A/B testing or a controlled rollout because offline metrics are not enough. Real users often behave differently than model judgments predict.

cards.front: 20. When is a simpler retrieval model better than a complex ranking stack?
cards.back: When the product value is mostly in correctness, speed, or predictable ordering rather than sophisticated personalization. Simpler systems are often easier to tune and more trustworthy.

author: Gemini
